tldr: Using a single consumer GPU (RTX 5070), the authors transferred Awa Odori dance from an ordinary monocular video to a commercial humanoid (Unitree G1), achieving up to 9.7 minutes of continuous rope-free dancing on a hard floor and dynamic handover with the factory walking controller.
hero_caption: Awa Odori dance performance on real Unitree G1 EDU hardware. On the left, a completely rope-free, continuous 9.7-minute free-standing performance; on the right, dancing with a slack safety rope attached for close-up filming. Both stably dance through the routine on a hard floor.
overview:
Making a humanoid robot perform an intense, expressive dance routine is a far harsher control problem than it looks. Simply replaying joint trajectories causes the robot to fall, as it must actively maintain the balance of its ~35 kg body in real time. Awa Odori, in particular, represents an almost worst-case stress test for control: keeping arms raised high continuously shifts the center of mass upward and shrinks the support polygon, while rapid, rhythmic single-support phases persist across a 43-second routine, allowing tiny errors to accumulate into catastrophic falls.

In this work, the authors built an end-to-end pipeline that extracts Awa Odori motions from a standard monocular tutorial video (e.g. from YouTube) and deploys them onto a commercial full-sized humanoid, the Unitree G1 EDU (29 degrees of freedom), achieving completely free-standing, rope-free execution on a hard floor. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, they adopted a disciplined 11-version deployment ladder where exactly one variable was modified per version and evaluated on real hardware.

This systematic approach pinpointed three fundamental obstacles that prevented deployment to real hardware. First, they discovered and resolved "metadata pollution," a failure where domain randomization during training silently leaks into export metadata and causes the real robot to destabilize. Second, by introducing an observation-noise model that captures low-frequency drift in the state estimator rather than just high-frequency jitter, they stopped the policy from chasing false odometry and falling. Third, rather than aggressively tuning the policy side, they showed that "reference motion engineering"—writing small scripts to scale motion amplitudes and transition into holding postures—is an extraordinarily cheap and decisive sim-to-real lever.

Ultimately, the resulting policies achieved three consecutive rope-free completions of the 43-second routine, a complete 46-second performance with a trained ending and automatic handoff back to the walking controller, and a continuous 9.7-minute rope-free performance looping the captured material. All pre-training and fine-tuning across the entire pipeline were completed on a single consumer GPU (RTX 5070, 12 GB).
contributions: A complete, reproducible pipeline from monocular video to free-standing, rope-free real-hardware performance on a hard floor (43 s completion, 46 s routine with ending and handoff, and 9.7 min continuous performance).

Identification of a previously unreported failure class where domain randomization silently corrupts deployment model artifacts and destabilizes hardware, along with automated prevention, detection, and repair procedures.
An observation-noise model capturing state-estimator drift that prevents the real robot from chasing false odometry and toppling, enabling the first sustained rope-free execution.

Demonstration that systematically editing and composing reference motions via scripts serves as a dramatically cheaper sim-to-real lever (requiring only ~2 GPU-hours of fine-tuning) than retraining policies from scratch.

A dynamic handover mechanism under commercial firmware constraints that safely bridges the torque-free window (45–140 ms) to transition seamlessly back and forth between the standard walking controller and the learned policy.

sections.heading: From Video to the Stage: Why Awa Odori?
sections.summary: Because of its high center of mass and continuous single-support phases, Awa Odori is one of the most grueling motions for a commercial humanoid. To bridge the final mile from simulation to real hardware, this work proposes a whole-body tracking pipeline trained on a single consumer GPU, guided by an 11-step single-variable ladder.
sections.details:
A humanoid robot is not just a motion replay machine. All 29 joints are driven by actuators, and the robot must autonomously maintain the balance of its ~35 kg body while executing choreography.

Awa Odori, a traditional festival dance from Tokushima, Japan, represents a near worst-case scenario for RL-based whole-body control. Holding both arms overhead for extended periods significantly raises the center of mass (CoM), drastically reducing the support margin at the feet. Furthermore, it contains rhythmic single-support phases across a continuous 43-second duration, allowing small discrepancies to accumulate into eventual falls.

The current standard approach is to train reference motion tracking policies via reinforcement learning (RL) inside parallel physics simulations and transfer them to real hardware (Sim-to-Real). However, the silent failure modes where a policy converges in simulation yet fails mysteriously on hardware, as well as the practical interventions needed to fix them, have remained poorly documented.

To tackle this, the authors conducted an 11-version ladder campaign on the Unitree G1 EDU, where each version modified exactly one variable from its parent and was evaluated on real hardware. Notably, all pre-training and fine-tuning were run on a single consumer GPU (GeForce RTX 5070, 12 GB) rather than a compute cluster.

sections.heading: Related Work and Positioning
sections.summary: Building upon imitation learning, sim-to-real transfer, and motion editing, this work takes a pragmatic approach: instead of altering policy architectures, it bridges the gap through artifact hygiene and reference motion editing.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of four main research areas:

### Learning-Based Whole-Body Control and Motion Imitation
Originating in character animation inside physics simulators, this field has recently expanded to real humanoid whole-body expression, teleoperation, and generalist controllers. While this work builds on the per-motion tracking framework BeyondMimic, it focuses on crane-free dynamic handoffs with standard walking controllers and generating multi-minute continuous performances from a single video.

### Sim-to-Real Transfer
Domain and dynamics randomization are standard tools, but conventional zero-mean per-step observation noise fails to capture the low-frequency drift inherent to real-world state estimators. This work introduces a minimal noise model that imparts drift tolerance without requiring the training of an auxiliary estimator.

### Motion Editing and Looping
Classical animation research made extensive use of signal processing and motion warping to stitch motions smoothly. This work repurposes these techniques for a control-engineering goal—keeping the physical robot inside its stable envelope and matching the gain regimes of the next controller—and combines them with fine-tuning into an exceptionally practical deployment mechanism.

### Deployment Artifacts
ONNX is widely adopted as an interchange format for trained models, typically self-contained with embedded metadata such as PD gains and default joint targets. However, the risk of training-time randomizations silently corrupting this metadata had never been reported.

sections.heading: From Video to Hardware: The Full Pipeline Architecture
sections.summary: The system spans six stages: monocular pose estimation, kinematic retargeting, RL training, ONNX export, and the onboard runtime. Because the reference motion is baked into the policy, motion editing is tightly coupled with low-cost fine-tuning.
sections.details:
The complete pipeline is structured across Stages A through F.

### 3.1 Stages A–B: From Video to Robot Motion
The input is a monocular instructional video of a professional dancer performing the female dance style (ordinary camera, no mocap suit) sourced from YouTube. PromptHMR estimates SMPL-X human mesh parameters frame-by-frame, extracting 1,032 clean frames (24 fps, 43.0 s). Next, GMR kinematically retargets this motion to the 29 degrees of freedom of the Unitree G1 (6 legs × 2, 3 waist, 7 arms × 2). This retargeting is purely kinematic with zero physics or balance awareness; making the motion physically feasible is left entirely to the subsequent RL stage.

### 3.2 Stage C: Editable Motion Files
The retargeted motion is saved as a plain text CSV with 1 row per frame and 36 columns (root position, quaternion, and 29 joint angles). Adopting this low-tech representation was a critical success factor: all subsequent choreographic modifications could be version-controlled, reproduced, and diffed with short NumPy scripts, completely bypassing complex animation software. The motion is resampled to the 50 Hz control frequency before training.

### 3.3 Stage D: Whole-Body Tracking Policy Training
Using BeyondMimic and rsl_rl (PPO) inside Isaac Lab, 2,048 environments are simulated in parallel (200 Hz physics, 50 Hz control). The actor is an MLP mapping a 160-dimensional input to 29-dimensional joint position targets. Training speeds on the RTX 5070 reach ~40,000–51,000 steps/s. Training from scratch takes 30k–75k iterations (several overnight runs), but fine-tuning from a checkpoint takes only 4k–6k iterations (just 1.5–2 hours).

### 3.4 Stages E–F: Export and Real-Hardware Runtime
The actor is exported to ONNX with 11 embedded metadata keys including PD gains and default joint targets. On the robot, the RoboJuDo runtime executes on the onboard Jetson, dynamically switching between the factory walking policy and the tracking policy in real time. Because the walking policy uses stiff gains (leg Kp between 150–300) while the dance policy uses compliant gains (leg Kp between 28–99), metadata accuracy and controller switching design are paramount.

captions.F2: Pose estimation from monocular video in Stage A. Following human detection with YOLOX-X and 2D keypoint estimation with PoseHRNet, SMPL-X meshes are recovered, accurately capturing Awa Odori traits like pigeon-toed foot lifts, high elbows, and two-beat limb coordination.
captions.F3: Stage D training environment in Isaac Lab. In one of the 2,048 parallel environments, the reference motion coordinate frames to be tracked are overlaid onto the simulated robot model controlled by the RL policy.
captions.F4: MuJoCo simulation verification prior to real-hardware deployment (Stage F). Using the exported ONNX policy and the exact runtime code deployed on hardware, the system confirms stable playback even with arms raised high overhead.

sections.heading: Three Decisive Sim-to-Real Interventions
sections.summary: Real-world success relied on three crucial interventions outside traditional policy learning: artifact hygiene, observation noise modeling low-frequency drift, and reference motion engineering.
sections.details:
Three decisive approaches proved essential for getting a policy that worked in simulation to succeed on real hardware.

### 4.1 Deployment Artifact Hygiene: The Metadata Pollution Problem
When a policy that performed flawlessly in simulation was exported and loaded onto the real robot, it caused subtle jitter, angled runaway drifts, and falls without throwing any errors. Investigation revealed that environment domain randomization had leaked into the metadata embedded during export (PD gains and default poses), writing corrupted values. Because the syntax was valid, deployment tools produced no warnings. The team eradicated this silent bug by isolating the export process from the training environment and adding CI validation and repair scripts that run in seconds.

### 4.2 Observation Noise Accounting for Estimator Drift
A real robot's onboard state estimator (odometry) does not just vibrate with high-frequency Gaussian noise; it accumulates position drift and carries persistent offsets (low-frequency drift). Policies trained on standard zero-mean noise place total trust in absolute position, causing the real robot to chase false odometry, skid sideways, and lose balance during single-support phases. By introducing an asymmetric drift noise model with persistent bias, the policy learned to selectively ignore odometry. While apparent tracking reward dropped in simulation, on real hardware this enabled the robot to survive rope-free for 22 seconds for the first time.

### 4.3 Reference Motion Engineering: Adjusting the Choreography Itself
The remaining failure modes stemmed from the choreography, not the policy. The authors addressed this by editing the reference motion CSV directly:
- **Amplitude Curriculum**: While keeping the iconic arm movements at 100%, foot lift amplitudes that caused instability were scaled down incrementally to 50% and 30%.
- **Engineered Endings**: Abrupt motion cuts at the end of the video were replaced with an artificial, smoothly interpolated transition back to the upright starting pose. This allowed safe handoffs back to the walking controller at rest and enabled seamless infinite looping.
- **Long-Horizon Composition**: By extracting stable expressive segments and smoothly stitching them together 16 times, a continuous 9.7-minute dance routine was generated from a single video.
These edits required only short scripts and roughly 2 GPU-hours of fine-tuning each—far cheaper than retraining policies from scratch.

sections.heading: The 11-Step Ladder: Discipline of Single-Variable Iteration
sections.summary: From v1 to v11, an 11-version ladder changed exactly one variable per version and evaluated each in simulation and on real hardware, isolating which interventions actually produced results.
sections.details:
To avoid haphazard trial-and-error during deployment, the team enforced a strict ladder protocol: change exactly one variable per version, and grade every single version in both simulation and real hardware.

- **Policy Robustness (v2, v3)**: Improved observation noise models produced policies resilient to real-world drift (v3 achieved 22 s of rope-free standing).
- **Reference Motion Engineering (v4, v5, v6, v8–v11)**: Reducing leg amplitudes enabled full 43-second completions (v5). Engineered endings allowed automated handoffs (v6) and scaling to 9.7-minute ultra-long loops (v10, v11).
- **Model Fidelity (v7)**: Added wrist mass payloads (~0.45 kg per hand) for the Dexterous Hands mounted on the physical robot.
- **Artifact Integrity**: Rigorous metadata repair was enforced across all versions from v3 onward.

Real-hardware trials followed strict safety rules: every version was first qualified on a crane, and only policies that passed were tested completely rope-free on the floor. This cleanly isolated and verified the qualitative effect of each intervention.

sections.heading: Training Dynamics: Apparent Shocks and True Rewards
sections.summary: Raw training logs reveal that performance collapses immediately after resuming fine-tuning are mere logging artifacts, and that high simulation rewards do not always correlate with hardware stability.
sections.details:
Analyzing training logs (e.g., TensorBoard) across all 11 versions revealed several practical insights for robotics practitioners.

### Unmasking the Apparent "Resume Shock"
Upon resuming fine-tuning from a checkpoint, rewards plummeted close to zero and episode lengths collapsed to 1.0 for the first ~20 iterations. While this appears to be catastrophic failure, it is an artifact of rsl_rl logging the mean over the "last 100 completed episodes." Because high-performing policies do not terminate until reaching 500 steps (~21 iterations), the first 20 iterations only reflect the statistics of the few environments that died immediately on reset. Recognizing this prevents practitioners from prematurely aborting valid fine-tuning runs.

### Reward Is Not the Ultimate Metric
Chasing raw simulation tracking reward numbers can be misleading. For instance, v3's final simulation reward (34.9–35.4) was lower than its parent v2 (40.3). This occurred because v3 was trained to ignore odometry drift, intentionally tolerating global position tracking errors (0.53 m). On real hardware, however, v3 was unquestionably the policy that remained standing stably.

At convergence, actor action noise standard deviations settled around 0.14–0.15; policies where this remained above 0.3 never succeeded on real hardware, providing a practical early-stopping signal.

sections.heading: Going Crane-Free: Dynamic Handover from the Factory Walker
sections.summary: To perform on stage without a crane, the authors designed a dynamic handover to walk in with the factory controller, transition smoothly into Awa Odori, and return to walking. It safely accommodates the firmware's 45–140 ms torque-free window.
sections.details:
For practical stage demonstrations, a robot cannot start dangling from a crane. It needs to walk to center stage using the factory walking controller, transition to Awa Odori on cue, and return to the walking controller to exit when finished.

### Navigating the Torque-Free Gap
Analysis of the G1's production firmware (v1.5.2) API revealed that transferring control to an external custom controller always forces a transition through a "damping (damp)" state. This inevitably introduces a 100–200 ms dead zone where no motor torque is commanded.

### The Blink, Stiff Catch, Crossfade Strategy
To render this torque-free gap harmless, the authors implemented a three-stage transition algorithm:
1. **Blink & Catch**: The runtime polls the switch request every 4 ms. The instant control is granted, it latches the current joint angles as targets with stiff bridge gains (ankle pitch/roll Kp $\geq$ 150) to catch the robot. This limits knee sagging to just $3\sim 5^\circ$ across the 45–140 ms gap, maintaining posture without any visible drop.
2. **Crossfade**: Attempting to interpolate posture directly toward the target starting pose caused the robot to pitch forward and fall. Instead, the robot is held frozen in place while its gains and torque commands smoothly crossfade over 3 seconds into the balance policy.
3. **Return**: At routine completion, the engineered ending ensures the robot is in a stationary upright stance, allowing the reverse transition back to the factory balanced stance (FSM 501) with complete stability.

This sequence was wrapped in a FastAPI HTTPS endpoint, enabling full automation: a single remote request (`/awa/dance`) starts the dance from a walk-ready idle, and an exit request (`/awa/finish`) hands control back to walking.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: 9.7 Minutes of Rope-Free Dancing
sections.summary: On a hard floor, the robot achieved three consecutive completions of the 43-second routine, a 46-second dance with automated handoff, and up to 9.7 minutes of continuous rope-free execution. Long-term position drift and flooring limitations were also mapped.
sections.details:
Real-world hardware trials on hard office flooring yielded dramatic milestones:

- **v5 Policy**: With the amplitude curriculum, it completed three consecutive 43-second runs completely rope-free.
- **v6 Policy**: Using the engineered ending, it concluded a 46-second performance and executed an automated handover to the walking controller with zero human touch.
- **v10/v11 Policies**: With the composed long-horizon reference motion, the robot danced continuously rope-free for 9.7 minutes (581 seconds) without human intervention.

### Position Drift During Long Performances
While the robot never fell during the 9.7-minute run, it exhibited a slow backward drift of about 1.5 m. This was caused by tiny balance recovery adjustments pushing the robot back several centimeters at a time, compounded by the fact that v10/v11 had disabled the drift-bias noise model of v3, leading the policy to chase accumulated errors in onboard odometry.

### Identifying Failure Boundaries
When deployed on compliant flooring (such as cushioned foam mats), the exact same policy destabilized and fell almost immediately. This represents a clear out-of-distribution (OOD) failure relative to the rigid-floor simulation, highlighting the need for floor compliance randomization in future work.

sections.heading: Seven Transferable Lessons for Robotics Practitioners
sections.summary: The findings extend well beyond Awa Odori. The authors synthesize seven general takeaways—including metadata integrity, low-frequency drift modeling, reference motion editing, and single-GPU viability—that apply directly to other humanoid platforms.
sections.details:
The project yielded seven universal lessons for researchers working on humanoid whole-body control:

- **1. Guard deployment artifacts against pollution**: Isolate export pipelines from training-time domain randomizations and enforce automated CI validation on ONNX metadata.
- **2. Model drift, not just jitter**: Real-world state estimators drift at low frequencies; injecting persistent bias noise trains the policy to avoid chasing odometry errors on hardware.
- **3. Amplitude scaling is the cheapest sim-to-real lever**: Writing a small script to shave 30% off leg amplitude in CSV is far cheaper and more effective than spending days tweaking policy rewards.
- **4. Choreograph your exit transitions**: Transitioning between controllers with vastly different gains is prone to failure during motion, but trivial at rest. Designing the motion to end in a quiet stance solves the handoff challenge.
- **5. Maintain discipline in one-motion-per-policy workflows**: Because changing choreography requires retraining, lightweight checkpoint resumption and automated versioning dictate development velocity.
- **6. Compliant flooring is a sharp OOD cliff**: Policies trained on rigid surfaces fail consistently on soft floors, making compliance randomization indispensable.
- **7. A single consumer GPU is enough**: A cluster is not required; an RTX 5070 (12 GB) is fully sufficient to train and deploy high-quality humanoid whole-body tracking.

The paper also notes gritty calibration insights: a standing IMU pitch reading of ~2 degrees reflects the robot's physical morphology rather than sensor fault, and manual joint zeroing breeds walking drift—relying on the official assisted calibration routine is strongly recommended.

sections.heading: Open Problems: Cumulative Drift and Monocular Limits
sections.summary: Open challenges remain for production deployment, including cumulative drift during multi-minute routines, pose tracking failures under self-occlusion, and adaptation to compliant floors.
sections.details:
Several clear limitations remain to be addressed in future work:

- **Correcting Cumulative Drift**: As seen in the 1.5 m backward migration over 9.7 minutes, drift accumulates over long routines. Future architectures need periodic re-anchoring motions or an outer-loop positional correction driven by the walking policy between dance segments.
- **Limits of Monocular Capture**: Fast-paced male dance styles could not be used due to severe self-occlusion causing monocular pose estimation to fail. Multi-view capture or temporal motion priors are needed.
- **Firmware-Level Handover**: Completely eliminating torque-free gaps requires manufacturer firmware to support seamless transitions directly to external command streams.
- **Cultural and Subjective Evaluation**: No objective metric measures whether the robot's performance is culturally authentic or aesthetically pleasing. Subjective evaluations by master dancers remain an obvious next step.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Expressive Humanoids Through Disciplined Engineering
sections.summary: From a single monocular video, the authors achieved long-duration, rope-free Awa Odori on a commercial humanoid. Disciplined single-variable iteration, motion editing, and proper noise modeling bridged the sim-to-real gap without exotic RL algorithms.
sections.details:
Starting from an open-source festival video on the internet, using open-source tools, a single consumer GPU, and a disciplined single-variable ladder methodology, this work realized an expressive, rope-free stage dance on a commercial humanoid.

The paper's core message is that bridging the sim-to-real gap did not require exotic new reinforcement learning algorithms. Instead, success came from pragmatic, rigorous engineering: validating deployment artifacts, modeling the true nature of real hardware noise, and editing reference motions before touching policy code. The deployment ladder and failure classifications presented provide a practical blueprint for any researcher seeking to deploy long-horizon expressive behaviors onto real humanoid robots.

takeaways: Reference motion engineering—scaling leg amplitudes or crafting static exit poses via short CSV scripts—is dramatically cheaper (~2 hours of fine-tuning) and more effective than endlessly adjusting RL policy rewards.
Guard against "metadata pollution," where training domain randomizations silently leak into exported ONNX metadata; isolate export pipelines and validate them in CI.
Because real-world state estimators exhibit low-frequency drift rather than just high-frequency jitter, injecting persistent bias noise prevents the policy from over-trusting odometry and toppling.

Safely handing over control between controllers with drastically different gains (compliant dance vs. stiff walking) is best achieved by choreographing the motion to end in a quiet stance and crossfading from a frozen pose.
Full-body 29-DOF imitation reinforcement learning—from pre-training to fine-tuning—can be fully completed on a single consumer GPU such as an RTX 5070 (12 GB).
limitations: During long-horizon continuous performances (~9.7 minutes), tiny balance recovery steps and odometry tracking cause an accumulated backward drift of approximately 1.5 meters, even though posture remains stable.
Relying on monocular pose estimation limits usable input motions; fast, athletic styles (such as male Awa Odori) fail during capture due to heavy limb crossings and self-occlusions.
Simulations assume rigid ground, causing the exact same policy to fail and fall immediately when tested on compliant surfaces like foam mats (vulnerability to out-of-distribution terrain).
